statement: Commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.
heath_proof: Let A, B be commensurable magnitudes; I say that A has to B the ratio which a number has to a number. For, since A, B are commensurable, some magnitude will measure them. Let it measure them, and let it be C. And, as many times as C measures A, so many units let there be in D; and, as many times as C measures B, so many units let there be in E. Since then C measures A according to the units in D, while the unit also measures D according to the units in it, therefore the unit measures the number D the same number of times as the magnitude C measures A; therefore, as C is to A, so is the unit to D; [VII. Def. 20] therefore, inversely, as A is to C, so is D to the unit. [cf. V. 7] Again, since C measures B according to the units in E, while the unit also measures E according to the units in it, therefore the unit measures E the same number of times as C measures B; therefore, as C is to B, so is the unit to E. But it was also proved that, as A is to C, so is D to the unit; therefore, ex aequali, as A is to B, so is the number D to E. [V. 22]  Therefore the commensurable magnitudes A, B have to one another the ratio which the number D has to the number E.
ai_proof_text:
10.5
**Statement:** Commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be commensurable magnitudes. By D10.1.1, commensurable magnitudes are those which are measured by the same measure; therefore some magnitude measures both A and B. Let C be such a magnitude, so that C measures A and C measures B.

**Step 2.** As many times as C measures A, so many units let there be in the number D; and as many times as C measures B, so many units let there be in the number E [D7.2, a number being a multitude composed of units]. Thus D and E are numbers; A is made up of as many magnitudes equal to C as there are units in D, and B is made up of as many magnitudes equal to C as there are units in E.

**Step 3.** Since C measures A, C is a part of A [D5.1]; and since the unit measures the number D, the unit is a part of D [D7.3]. Now C measures A according to the units in D, while the unit measures D according to the units in it; hence the unit measures D the same number of times that C measures A. Therefore C is the same part of A that the unit is of D, and consequently, as C is to A, so is the unit to D [D7.20].

**Step 4.** Since, as C is to A, so is the unit to D, therefore, inversely, as A is to C, so is D to the unit [5.7, Porism].

**Step 5.** Again, since C measures B according to the units in E, while the unit measures E according to the units in it, the unit measures E the same number of times that C measures B. Therefore C is the same part of B [D5.1] that the unit is of E [D7.3]; hence, as C is to B, so is the unit to E [D7.20].

**Step 6.** There are now three magnitudes A, C, B and three others D, unit, E equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two are in the same ratio: as A is to C, so is D to the unit (Step 4), and as C is to B, so is the unit to E (Step 5). Therefore, ex aequali, as A is to B, so is D to E [5.22].

**Step 7.** Therefore the commensurable magnitudes A and B have to one another the ratio which the number D has to the number E. Q.E.D.
